title: Unprecedented Lower Over-potential for CO2 Electro-reduction on Copper oxide Anchored to Graphene Oxide Microstructures
abstract: Efficient conversion of CO2 into chemical feedstock and fuels via electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (ECO2R) has perpetuated ambitious and broad research interests. Herein, we report the design and synthesis of copper oxide anchored to graphene oxide (Cu/CuxO.GO) porous microstructures via a simple and atom-economical DC electrophoresis approach that exhibit excellent electro-catalytic activity toward ECO2R. A systematic rationalisation of the several physico-chemical parameters associated with the fabrication of porous Cu/CuxO.GO network, viz. composition, the extent of defects in GO and the proportion of oxide contents in Cu/ CuxO was explored to understand their impact on the electro-catalytic activity of copper plus GO-based composites. The porous and asymmetric Cu/CuxO.GO nano-composite with optimised oxide content, and metal-GO interactions exhibit an excellent activity for CO2 electroreduction into CO and ethane with a respective Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) of ca. 40% and 4% at an applied potential of just -0.28 V (vs NHE) in a CO2 saturated acetonitrile solution. Comparison of the overpotential specific F.E. values with the ones reported for similar investigations suggests that the electro-catalytic performance of the Cu/CuxO.GO network is significantly better than that observed for various state of the art electro-catalysts recently designed for the ECO2R.

A B S T R A C T
Efficient conversion of CO2 into chemical feedstock and fuels via electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (ECO2R) has perpetuated ambitious and broad research interests. Herein, we report the design and synthesis of copper oxide anchored to graphene oxide (Cu/CuxO.GO) porous microstructures via a simple and atom-economical DC electrophoresis approach that exhibit excellent electro-catalytic activity toward ECO2R. The porous and asymmetric Cu/CuxO.GO nano-composite with optimised oxide content, and metal-GO interactions exhibit an excellent activity for CO2 electroreduction into CO and ethane with a respective Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) of ca. 40% and 4% at an applied potential of just -0.28 V (vs NHE) in a CO2 saturated acetonitrile solution. sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The exponentially increasing global CO2 concentration in the atmosphere has stimulated an intense research activity towards the development of economically viable technologies for environmental remediation and search for carbon-neutral energy sources. In this regard, addressing CO2 problem on the lines of the natural photosynthetic process continues to be a fascinating challenge for the researchers [1,2]. Especially, conversion of CO2 to CO, an essential component of synthesis gas (CO + H2), a precursor for the industrial Fisher-Tropsch process, is at the centre stage of substantial research activities in this direction. So far, several approaches for sequestration of CO2 and its conversion into the useful chemicals or fuels have been reported [3–6]. Among these approaches, the electrochemical method is considered as potentially more efficient and economical [7,8]. In this context, the design of a stable and efficient electro-catalyst that can ensure electroreduction of CO2 to CO with high faradaic efficiency (F.E.) at lower overpotentials continues to attract significant attention of the material electrochemists.
Among the range of materials tested by Hori [9,10] and other
researchers for electroreduction of CO2 to CO, Au has been found to exhibit the highest F.E. of ca. 81-93% in aqueous electrolyte solutions. Recently, Liu et al. [11] demonstrated that with triangularly shaped Ag nanoparticles (NPs) plus carbon black composite, F.E. for CO2 to CO conversion could be excelled to more than 96% in 0.1 M KHCO3. However, the cost and stability concerns of Au and Ag warrant the design of stable, efficient and economic potential alternative to these noble metal electrocatalysts. This is a must to make the electrochemical transformation of CO2 to CO industrially scalable and economically viable. The lower solubility of CO2 in water, the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), and multiple pathways available for the ECO2R pose additional challenges in the selective and efficient electroconversion of CO2 to CO in aqueous electrolytes. In this regard, use of aprotic media that besides ensuring better solubility of CO2 (e.g. the solubility of CO2 in acetonitrile is eight times that in water) also allow the access to more negative potentials and facilitates selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO [1°]. For example, Zeng et al. [12] revealed a whopping 99% of F.E. using Pt NPs supported on TiO2-InP composites in an ionic liquid medium.

reaction (ECO2R), copper and its alloys exhibit unique ability to reduce CO2 into a variety of hydrocarbon products and CO. Although, in aqueous media, Cu based electrodes favour the production of significant quantities of hydrocarbons from ECO2R [9,13], in absence of competitive HER these show a good selectivity and efficiency for electroreduction of CO2 to CO. The conversion efficiency values reported for the various state of the art electrocatalysts in CO2 saturated aprotic/organic/ionic liquid solutions is still much lower than that desired for large scale conversion of CO2 to CO. However, the various experimental and theoretical studies reported so far about ECO2R suggest that the F.E. for CO production with electrocatalysts can be appreciably improved through appropriate tuning of the electro-catalyst surface. This has been experimentally confirmed especially by Kanan and co-workers [13] by demonstrating that F.E. for CO production over Cu electrodes varies as a function of Cu2O shell thickness. Tang et al. [14] have also demonstrated the importance of surface morphology of Cu based materials in affecting their selectivity and efficiency toward electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 to CO.
To our knowledge, 38% of F.E. obtained at an applied potential of less than -0.3 V vs NHE is still the highest value reported so far for Cubased electrocatalysts [13], requiring stringent experimental conditions for their preparation and use for ECO2R. All these facts and concerns have intensified the quest for the design of low cost, stable and selective copper-based electrocatalysts for ECO2R. In the ensuing search, the results from electro-catalytic investigations on Cu-nanodeposits confined over conducting substrate have been very encouraging [15]. A strong synergism between GO and metal nanoparticle based electrocatalysts has been reported to bridge the energy requirement and product specificity in ECO2R [16–18]. It is reported that GO and other carbon-based supports, like carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and nitrogendoped CNTs appreciably enhance the stability and the catalytic activity of a copper-based catalyst towards ECO2R [19–21]. It is relevant to state here that the oxygen functionalities on the GO surface have been predicted/reported to alter the interaction between analyte species and the support materials which have been observed to play a crucial role in the analyte-specific electrocatalytic activity of GO-based metal nanocomposites [16–18].
Through the present article, we report the electrophoretic synthesis of a Cu and GO-based nanocomposite (Cu/CuxO.GO) exhibiting high stability, efficiency and selectivity toward ECO2R to CO. A simple, highyielding electrochemical deposition approach for the production of Cu/ CuxO.GO, wherein the morphology as well as composition of the composite can be tuned through easy to carry variations in the synthetic parameters [22–25] is discussed. The presented synthetic strategy besides alleviating the requirement of harmful chemicals ensures the electro-deposition of the electro-catalyst at potentials that are significantly lower than those required for similar procedures reported in the recent past [26]. We demonstrate that over Cu/CuxO.GO nanocomposite with optimal activity, ECO2R onset potential of ca. -0.05 V vs NHE and F.E. of ca. 40% at an applied potential of -0.28 V vs NHE is achievable for CO2 to CO electro-conversion. While the observed onset potential for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO is unprecedentedly the lowest, the F.E. is the highest reported so far for ECO2R over metalbased electrocatalysts in general and Cu-based in particular at such low over-potentials.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and Chemicals
sections.text:
All the chemicals used for the synthesis and electrochemical measurements were of analytical grade and unless otherwise mentioned were used as such without further purification. Tri-sodium citrate (TSC) (99%) was procured from Merck, India. Graphene oxide dispersion in water (4 mg/mL) and tetra-butyl ammonium tetra-fluoroborate (TBABF4, 99%) were procured from Sigma Aldrich. Prior to its use,
TBABF4 was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C and stored in vacuum desiccator. Acetonitrile (ACN) of HPLC grade (with water contents of ca. 1000 ppm) was procured from Fischer Scientific and stored over activated molecular sieves before using it for electrochemical measurements. Ultrapure CO2, CO and N2 gases were procured from Sigma Gases, New Delhi and were passed through a filter equipped with an oxygen trap, gas purifier and moisture trap to remove the traces of impurities (Prama Instruments Pvt. Ltd.) before their use for electrochemical measurements. A copper metal rod (99.9% pure, metal basis) was procured from Alfa Aesar. Carbon fibre paper (CFP) sheets (TGPH120) were procured from Nickunj Exim Entp. Pvt. Ltd. India.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of Cu/CuxO.GO nano-composites
sections.text:
Different Cu/CuxO.GO composites were synthesised via a modified DC electrophoresis approach recently reported by us for the synthesis of varied shaped plasmonic Cu/CuxO nanoparticles (NPs) [27]. Typically, a copper rod (6 mm diameter) polished with fine emery paper followed by 10 s immersion in 10% HNO3 and then rinsed several times with copious amount of acetone and deionised water was used as a sacrificial anode. Pt rod (0.2 mm diameter) or CFP (with 4 mm x 4 mm of surface area exposed to electrolyte) was used as collecting cathode (i.e. to deposit micro-CuxO composites). The electrodes were immersed in a conventional electrochemical cell containing continuously stirred aqueous tri-sodium citrate (200 mM) solution along with a known amount of GO aqueous suspension (0.3 mg/mL diluted from stock solution with concentration of 4 mg/mL) maintained at a constant temperature of ca. 40 °C (± 0.1 °C). A constant voltage was applied between Cu anode and Pt rod or CFP cathode using a Keithley (2231A-30-3) triple channel DC power supply (Tektronix).
The colour of the solution changed from bluish to reddish-brown after the potential was applied. The reaction was stopped by switching off the power supply after the stipulated time intervals. For the samples prepared with Pt as a cathode, the reaction product was tapped-off from the Pt surface, transferred into deionised water and centrifuged for ca. 10 minutes followed by several washes with water and methanol, consecutively to remove the excess of TSC, if any, adsorbed on nanocomposite surface. The composite was then transferred into Petri dish, dried in vacuum oven and scratched off as a dry powder. The samples prepared using CFP cathode were collected in the form of electro-deposited films on CFP, the films were rinsed with water, and then nitrogen dried before their characterisation or use in electrochemical measurements. Based on the cathode used and the absence or presence of GO in electrolyte medium, the electrodeposited samples are referred to as pCu/CuxO(PtRod) {‘p’ stands for powder, the state these samples were obtained from their synthesis, ‘parenthesis’ denotes the type of substrate used in the synthesis of the materials}, pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) {on Pt cathode and GO in solution in addition to tri-sodium citrate}, fCu/CuxO(CFP) {‘f’ denotes film, the state these samples were obtained on the CFP in their synthesis}, and fCu/CuxO.GO(CFP) {using CFP cathode in presence of GO}.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material Characterization
sections.text:
Crystallinity and lattice parameters of materials were analysed by Xray diffractometer (XRD) Bruker model D8 Advance with Cu Kα (λ = 1.54 Å) as excitation radiation and a scan speed of 0.2 sec/increment and scan from 2θ = 10° to 90°. For the samples obtained using Pt cathode, XRD patterns were recorded on the powder samples collected from the synthesis bath, whereas for the samples obtained using CFP cathode, XRD measurements were directly performed over the films electrodeposited onto the CFP. The field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM) attached with Oxford-EDS system IE 250X max 80 with latest 80 mm2 SDD detector model FEI Quanta 200 was used to determine morphology and elemental composition of the prepared materials. Raman analysis of the composites was carried on Renishaw
plc micro Raman spectrometer with 514 nm laser. Gas chromatography (GC) measurements were done on NUCON 1765 gas chromatogram operating with following method; injection temperature: 190 °C, TCD detector temperature: 210 °C, FID detector temperature: 190 °C with a carrier gas flow rate of 25 mL/min, and temperature ramps of 70 °C - 215 °C. X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) data was collected on Omicron ESCA + instrument manufactured by Oxford Instruments, Germany. The detector used was Argus with a mean radius of 124 mm (Inner radius-120.8 mm and outer radius- 127.2 mm) and the angle between analyzer and source was 90 degrees. The source used was a monochromatic Al Kα radiation (hν =1.4 keV) with a resolution of ∼0.60 eV. The instrument was operated at 15 kV and 20 mA. For short scans, the pass energy was 20 eV, while for the survey, it was 50 eV.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
All the electrochemical measurements were carried out on Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT302 N with standard three electrode system in a single chamber conventional cell or in a custom-made 2-chambered cell with an anionic membrane from Dioxide Materials USA, separating catholyte from anolyte. CFP modified with electro-catalyst was used as working electrode, while Pt wire and a Pt loop were employed as a quasi-reference and counter electrode, respectively. Both Pt wire and wire loops electrodes were well-polished, cleaned and dried before their use for electrochemical measurements.
Working electrodes for ECO2R were fabricated in following five different ways; (i) electrodeposited samples obtained on CFP were used as such without any modifications (weight of the electrodeposit on CFP was obtained by subtracting weight of unmodified CFP from that of modified CFP), (ii) the electrodeposited powders obtained at Pt (same amount to that obtained for CFP modified electrodes) were re-dispersed in 200 μL water, 600 μL isopropanol and 10 μL Nafion (as binder) solution and sonicated for 30 minutes and then 50 μL of this suspension was drop casted on a fresh piece (4 mm x 4 mm) of CFP (to keep similar substrate for ECO2R measurements), dried under IR-lamp before using them for studying ECO2R. To understand the role of electro-deposition of a film versus the traditional drop-casting, i.e. mode of electrode fabrication, three more electrodes were fabricated in the following manner. (iii) CFP, pre-modified by drop-casting few microliters of GO suspension on it to make total GO content same as in other materials (3 mg) and used as cathode for electro-deposition of Cu/CuxO NPs on its surface, and the resulting electrode is labelled as fCu/CuxO@GO(CFP) (‘f’ denotes film; the state these materials were obtained on CFP from synthesis,‘@’ denotes the immediate layer beneath the active catalyst layer), (iv) another electrode was fabricated by layering GO on CFP and then coating with a second layer of Cu/CuxO(PtRod) NPs to study the effect of physical mixing of copper oxide and GO as compared to electrochemical interaction between the copper oxides and the GO and was named as pCu/CuxO@GO(CFP) (‘p’ denotes powder; the state these materials were obtained from their synthesis bath,‘@’ representing physical contact, i.e. layer on layer).
Finally, to understand the synergism between Cu/CuxO and GO, another electrode (v) was fabricated. For this, the same amount of GO suspension was hand painted on clean CFP, dried under vacuum, and the obtained electrode was labelled as GO. All care was taken to mask the rest of the electrode surface so that for all the fabricated electrodes identical area of CFP cathode is exposed for sample loading and hence for electrochemical measurements. Also, ECSA was determined from capacitance measurement calculated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves recorded in capacitive region of these samples at different scan rates.
ACN with 0.1 M TBABF4 as a supporting electrolyte was chosen as an electrolyte medium for studying ECO2R. For this, CO2 gas was purged (for 30 minutes) through the electrolyte medium taken in a gastight electrochemical cell (four-neck glass cell for signle compartment and a custom made Teflon cell for 2-chambered cell) with the provision of fixing a Tedlar bag on the top of the cell through one of the necks for
sampling the ECO2R gaseous products for their analysis using gas chromatography. All the potentials presented in this report were calibrated to the reference potential of normal hydrogen electrode (NHE) by using the ferrocene/ferrocenium couple as an internal standard [28–30]. For this, ferrocene (ca. 3 mg) was added into the ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 electrolyte medium analysed previously, and CVs were recorded using CFP as a working electrode. Thus obtained
= +E1/2 (E E ) 2 red ox was equated with standard redox potential of ferrocene in similar electrolyte medium (E1/2 of ferrocene in ACN/0.1 M tetrabutyl ammonium perchlorate (TBAP) = +0.31 V vs SCE) [29] and the potential scale of all the other CVs then calibrated accordingly. Moreover, all the CVs were corrected for IR drops which is highly important parameters in case of electrochemical analysis using organic solvents. For this, electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) at OCP from 10 kHz to 0.1 Hz was recorded to find the solution resistance, and this resistance was used for the estimation and correction of IR drop of CV curves with Nova 2.4 software.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis and characterisation of Cu/CuxO.GO nano-composites
sections.text:
A simple and facile electrochemical dissolution approach recently employed by us for the crafting of Cu/CuxO nanostructures [27] was extended for the synthesis of Cu/CuxO.GO composite. Similar methods have been reported in the literature for the synthesis of CuxO NPs, but the proposed methodologies require higher currents density/high voltages and use of strongly acidic or basic electrolyte medium [26]. For the present work, we employed very mild reaction conditions like electrolyte bath temperature of 40 °C, TSC as an additive and DC voltage as low as 15 V applied between Cu anode and Pt rod or CFP cathode in the presence of GO suspension. Under these operating conditions, copper rod undergoes anodic dissolution to form copper ions which then migrate to the cathode under the influence of applied potential. The electro-generated Cu2+cations form complex with TSC ions and are then reduced to Cu° at cathode or are converted into copper hydroxide, i.e. Cu (OH)2 on their reaction with water. The Cu (OH)2 produced, may transform into either CuO or Cu2O.
We have noticed that TSC, as an additive, plays an essential role in the synthesis of copper oxide nanostructures. It not only acts as a stabiliser to control the growth of copper oxide into nano-dimension but also facilitates the electro-dissolution of copper at lower potentials which otherwise requires a very high DC voltage. On anodic polarisation, copper dissolves into Cu2+ and is consumed at cathode forming Cu0. While in absence of TSC higher energy is required to keep the reaction going, the presence of citrate ions in the solution and their complexation with Cu2+ to stabilise it facilitates and thereby enhances the Cu electro-dissolution [31,32]. Furthermore, it favours the selective formation of Cu2O, thereby offering an additional parameter that can be employed to control the oxide contents (i.e. O/Cu ratio) in the Cu/ CuxO NPs. Our synthetic methodology presents an excellent synthetic
exploitation of TSC wherein its multiple potentialities are employed for facilitating the synthesis, tuning of the composition and stabilisation of the nanostructures (copper oxide in the present study). This feature, adds another dimensionality to the potential utility of citrate moieties that are already reported to play a critical role as capping ligands, reducing agent and pH controlling additives [33,34] for the synthesis of nanocomposites.
Fig. 1 shows XRD patterns of Cu/CuxO and their composites with GO synthesised by electrochemical deposition method. The major diffraction peaks suggest the formation of mixed phases of CuO, Cu2O, and metallic Cu corresponding to the JCPDS file Nos. 48-1548, 05-0667, and 85-1326, respectively. The XRD patterns for two of the samples electrodeposited as powder over Pt cathode are shown in the left panel of Fig. 1, while those for the sample electrodeposited on CFP are shown in the right panel of the same figure. XRD pattern of pCu/CuxO(PtRod) depicts three major diffraction peaks positioned at 43°, 51° and 74° corresponding to (111), (200), and (220) planes of the fcc crystal structure of metallic copper with space group of Fm3m (JCPDS No. 85- 1326). Few minor peaks located at 36°, 42° and 61° related to diffraction from (111), (200) and (220) planes of fcc Cu2O (JCPDS No. 05- 0667) can also be noticed in these X-ray diffractograms. Interestingly, upon addition of GO {in case of pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod)}, comparatively more oxide phase of copper than that observed in the absence of GO {i.e. pCu/CuxO(PtRod)} was noticed. The XRD pattern of pCu/CuxO.GO (PtRod) depicts diffraction peaks positioned at 36º, 42º, 61º and 73º related to reflections from (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of Cu2O phase. Besides, few peaks located at 35º, 38º, 49° and 61° corresponding to diffraction from (11Ῑ), (111), (200), and (113) planes of monoclinic CuO (JCPDS file No. 48-1548) along with few significant peaks from metallic Cu {same as pCu/Cu2O(PtRod) NPs} are also observable. Thus, the presence of GO in the electrophoretic setup seems to favour the oxide phase than the metallic Cu in pCu/CuxO(PtRod) NPs, which could be a manifestation of oxygen group transfer from GO to copper.
The XRD patterns of samples electrodeposited at CFP cathode are shown in right panel of Fig. 1. The strong diffraction peaks located at ca. 55° in XRD pattern of the samples prepared using CFP as a cathode corresponds to the graphitic carbon planes of carbon fibres from the surface of CFP. Similar to the samples obtained at Pt rod cathode, the electrodeposit prepared at CFP cathode also depicts higher contents of oxide phase in the presence of GO than in its absence. However, the change in cathode material from Pt rod to CFP does not appreciably change the crystallographic phases of the electrodeposit. These observations establish the influence of GO on phase preference of copper/ copper oxide nano-structures that can be attributed to the interaction between GO and copper, wherein the reduction of GO preferentially favours the crystallization of the oxide phase of the metal during electrophoretic deposition of the later. This variation in crystalline phases influences the electrocatalytic activity of these copper-based electro-catalyst materials [35,36]. Table 1 summarises the presence of major crystallographic phases as a function of cathode material as well as presence or absence of GO along with other physicochemical parameters. A charge transfer effect on addition of GO manifests in the
phase change of the catalyst. XPS (SI-1) results show that both Cu (0) and Cu(I) are present in pCu/CuxO(PtRod) with a ratio of 1:4.5 for the area under O1s peak and Cu 2p peak from the survey spectrum. The ratio of area under O 1s peak and Cu 2p peak changes to 1:2.8 in pCu/ CuxO.GO(PtRod) and shows exclusive Cu(I) oxidation state.
FESEM images depicts the nanomorphology of the catalysts as shown in the images recorded for these nanocomposites shown in Fig. 2. As obvious from the FESEM images, most of the samples show porous microstructures with cone shapes that are more prominent in the case of pCu/CuxO(PtRod) electrodeposit. The FESEM images recorded for pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) depict Cu/CuxO particles anchored to the GO sheets. Similar microstructures assembled on the carbon fibres can be seen in case of the samples obtained with CFP cathode {figure 2 (c and d)}. For pCu/CuxO@GO(CFP), similar features as that of pCu/ CuxO(PtRod) sample are noticed, however, with the presence of GO sheets {figure 2 (e)}. The high-resolution images of these samples shown in insets indicate fine spherical particles of Cu/CuxO self-assembled as cone-shaped porous microstructures. For comparison, FESEM image of pristine GO hand painted on CFP was also recorded and is shown in Figure SI-2. The image distinctly shows graphene sheets throughout the scanned area.
To explore the nature of interactions, and the state of different components in the electroproduced composites, Raman spectroscopy measurements were carried out for the pellets of as synthesised samples. It is well documented that interaction between CuxO and GO often leads to charge transfer which manifests into the reduction of GO. Fig. 3 depicts an overlay of Raman spectra recorded for Cu/CuxO.GO electrodeposits prepared and tested for the present work. For all the samples, the depicted spectra include peaks characteristic to pristine GO sample, i.e. peaks positioned at 1350 cm-1 corresponding to D band (related to degree of order/disorder due to a breathing k-point phonon of A1g symmetry) and at 1590 cm-1corresponding to G band (related to the E2g phonon of sp2 hybridized carbon atoms, which is an indicator of the stacking structure) [37,38]. In the spectra corresponding to pCu/ CuxO.GO(PtRod) composites, a significant enhancement in D band and lowering in G band as compared to pristine GO indicating the formation of a composite between Cu/CuxO and GO is noticed. Furthermore, the ratio of intensities of D band to that of G band (i.e. ID/IG ratio) estimated from the Raman spectra suggest a peculiar trend that very well matches our inferences from XRD analysis. Particularly, sample electrodeposited with Pt cathode, i.e. pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) shows the highest ID/IG intensity ratio of 1.31:1, followed by pCu/CuxO.GO(CFP) with a ratio of 1.01:1, then fCu/CuxO@GO(CFP) with ID/IG = 0.93:1 and GO with ID/IG = 0.92:1. The values of ID/IG estimated for the synthesised composites are also enlisted in Table 1. Pertinent to mention that higher ID/IG ratio reflects a greater extent of interaction between metal and GO support.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical Investigations
sections.text:
For ECO2R, the choice of solvent plays an essential role as it decides not only the reaction mechanism but also the product profile and
reaction kinetics of the overall process. As solvent for ECO2R, so far published reports suggest that ACN influences the course of the electrodics by ensuring better availability of CO2 near electrode surface [39–43]. Besides, the well-established and well documented mechanistic aspects associated with ECO2R into CO in ACN [39,43] were the primary reasons for our selection of ACN as solvent for ECO2R for the
present investigations. Reaction parameters and conditions as followed in these above-cited reports [39,43] were replicated for the presented investigations. This approach was purposefully ensured so that the results from current study, especially the overpotential values and faradaic efficiencies can be readily compared with those reported in these cited investigations [39,43].

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Choice of deposit collector in electrodeposition, Pt rod vs CFP
sections.text:
The host substrate plays a vital role in electrophoretic deposition as it not only guides the phenomenon of NP growth but also affects the morphology of the electrodeposit. For the present work, we explored the effect of collection substrate viz. Pt rod or CFP over the morphology and electrocatalytic performance of Cu/CuxO, CuxO.GO nano-composites. For the sake of clarity, catalytic activities of the catalyst prepared with and without GO were compared separately. All CVs presented are with current normalized to their ECSA. The literature reported specific capacitance value of 20 microfarad for Cu-metal was used for the estimation of ECSA from capacitance current measurements in the CVs at changing scan rates (SI-3).
Fig. 4 (left panel) shows comparison of current-potential curves for ECO2R on Cu/CuxO (without GO support) obtained at similar phased samples synthesised over Pt rod and CFP cathodes. It suggests that the samples of Cu/CuxO prepared with Pt rod cathode are catalytically more active than the ones prepared with CFP cathode showing lower overpotential and higher current density for CO2 conversion. The difference in activities was deciphered by analysing several reaction products in the gaseous phase. While with pCu/CuxO(PtRod) prepared with Pt rod cathode F.E.CO was observed to be ca. 25%, fCu/CuxO(CFP)
prepared with CFP cathode exhibited F.E.CO of just 14% that too at higher negative overpotential (refer, Section 3.4). A similar trend was noted for the samples prepared in the presence of GO too, where an impressive F.E.CO of 40% was obtained for pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) prepared with Pt cathode as compared to only 14% of F.E.CO for the composite prepared with CFP cathode {fCu/CuxO.GO(CFP)}.
CFP which is also used as a gas diffusion layer (GDL) has high surface area due to its porous network and is expected to impart better activity to the catalyst prepared when employed as a collection substrate [44,45]. However, the observed trend has been contrary to the expected and can be explained on the basis of differences in the morphology, shape, and crystallinity induced by differing surface attachments offered by Pt rod and CFP. These differences can also be attributed to the extent and strength of adsorption of the deposition layer on to the host substrate, which is expected to be stronger in case of direct deposition on CFP than drop cast. Hence, the samples prepared with Pt rod cathode possess more porosity and independent structures, leading to better activity compared to those prepared with CFP cathode. The higher porosity of the catalyst obtained with Pt rod cathode than that of CFP can also be on account of higher hydrogen evolution on Pt surface than CFP cathode during electrodeposition of the nano-structures from aqueous TSC solution under applied potentials. The shape of the composite prepared with Pt rod instead of CFP is significantly different (refer, Fig. 2). While the use of Pt rod cathode leads to Cu/CuxO with sharper ends, CFP cathode produces less spiky samples with lower electrocatalytic activity. A similar observation was also noticed for the samples prepared in the presence of GO where pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) show better activity than fCu/CuxO.GO(CFP) in terms of lower onset as well as higher F.E. towards CO production.
It is pertinent to mention here that the use of metallic counter electrode (such as Pt-wire loop in the present case) in a single-chambered cell may interfere with the analysis of ECO2R, where in general, the reduction products generated at cathode undergo oxidation. We repeated the ECO2R measurements in a custom designed gas-tight two chambered cell fitted with sustainion from Dioxide materials USA as an anionic membrane. Though we could record CVs for CO2 reduction with all the electrocatalytic materials designed for the current work as the active electrode surface, the membrane was observed to perforate during prolonged electrolysis experiments. The problem was not only for anionic membranes; Nafion 117 was also observed to be unstable under similar conditions, and ACN solutions turned yellow after some time, say half an hour, in bulk electrolysis. The selection of appropriate membrane materials that can exhibit desired stability in two chambered cells for CO2 reduction under higher negative potentials needs further researching.
Fig. 5 shows the CVs recorded over pCu/CuxO(PtRod), pCu/Cu2O.GO (PtRod) and fCu/Cu2O.GO(CFP) in CO2 saturated ACN in a two chambered electrochemical cell. The depicted CVs indicate that the relative
electrocatalytic activity of the samples is not affected while shifting the experimentation from one compartment to a two-compartment cell. However, compared to one compartment cell, an appreciable shift of about 500 mV towards more negative potentials was noticed for the peak potential of ECO2R in the two compartment cell. This can be attributed to the excess IR drop expected for the two compartment setup. In view of the limited stability of the membrane employed in our two compartment cell, we were able to collect gaseous products only over small intervals of time of ca. 15 min., post which the membrane would break. Therefore, we restricted our experiments with two chambered electrolytic cell to the most electro-catalytic samples only. From product analysis in these experiments we found that there is 7.9% increase in production of CO, 3% increase in CH4 and production of ethylene with 16% while increase in H2 evolution was comparatively much higher (ca. 29%) than what was observed with single chambered electrolytic cell.

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Effect of electrode fabrication method on ECO2R activity
sections.text:
While doing the preliminary experiments, we noticed that the strategy employed for electrode fabrication has a profound effect on the ECO2R activity of the electro-catalyst. In general, several researchers including us have preferred a layer by layer coating of electro-catalyst over the support material [45–46] whereas few others have preferred a mixed form of the electrocatalyst and a support material [47]. However, such a choice remains a moot point and is most of the time not justified with enough experimentation. Therefore, to avoid such ambiguities in the case of presented experiments, we compared the electro-
catalysis results for different ways of fabricating the working electrode. Figure SI-4 (left panel) displays an overlay of CVs recorded for the electrodes fabricated in three different ways viz. fCu/CuxO@GO, pCu/ CuxO@GO and fCu/CuxO.GO. Electrode pCu/CuxO@GO was fabricated as follows: CFP was first painted with GO support material by dropcasting the fixed quantity of GO suspension followed by drying under IR lamp and then adding a layer of pCu/CuxO(PtRod) catalyst layer by drop cast method. Thus, fabricated electrode was dried and used as cathode for CO2 electro-reduction. Electrode with fCu/CuxO@GO was also fabricated as layer over layer, here Cu/CuxO NPs were electrodeposited on a drop cast GO layer on CFP. Hence, a set of catalysts, all having Cu/ CuxO in contact with GO but fabricated either as physical layer over layer, electrochemically driven Cu/CuxO over physically coated GO and electrochemically co-deposited Cu/CuxO and GO. The set gives an idea about the best way to fabricate an electrode for ECO2R, which most often has been neglected while considering its effect on the catalytic activity.
As noted from Figure SI-4 (left panel), among these three electrodes, the electrode fabricated by simultaneous electrochemical deposition of Cu/CuxO and GO on CFP shows the lowest onset and peak potentials for ECO2R with F.E.CO of 15%. Comparatively the pCu/CuxO@GO depicting more negative peak and onset potentials with F.E. of 15% was found to be less active than the electrode obtained through simultaneous deposition of Cu/CuxO and GO followed by fCu/CuxO@GO that gives similar F.E.CO of 15% but with more negative peak and onset potentials. Therefore, we can conclude that the composite form of Cu/ CuxO and GO acts as a better catalyst especially when compared to the electrodes fabricated via layer-by-layer assembly, suggesting the possible involvement of synergistic effect towards the enhancement of electrocatalytic activity.
A careful morphological inspection of fCu/CuxO@GO from Fig. 2(f), reveals that the copper oxide electro-catalyst remains buried under the GO layer exposing lesser surface of electro-catalyst accessible for the electro-catalysis process thereby making it the least active electro-catalyst system after GO; as GO is rich in negative sites, the approach of copper ions would be more in this case due to electrostatic forces. Another interesting observation we noted was that the sample pCu/ CuxO(PtRod) shows lower electrocatalytic activity when it is present as a physical mixture (layer-by-layer assembly) with GO support material than the neat pCu/CuxO(PtRod) deposited directly on the CFP substrate. The fall in activity could be a simple outcome of insertion of a less active layer of GO between CFP and Cu/CuxO that leads to the longer tunnelling distances in such cases. This further validates the hypothesis that the layer-by-layer assembly may not always result in activity boosting and negative effects can also be noted as presented in this study. The voltammetric features recorded for the ECO2R over various composites synthesised and tested during the current work were analysed in light of various structure-composition aspects as suggested by their morphological and spectroscopic features; some of these are discussed in the following sub-sections.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Effect of GO support and the extent of GO reduction
sections.text:
The synergism offered by the support and the electro-active components of composite electrodes has been well established and was also noted in the present study. Graphite composites are well-known to enhance the catalytic activity of metal and metal oxide NPs as a catalyst for ECO2R [37,47]. Addition of GO was observed to elevate the catalytic activity of copper oxide nanostructures (see Figure SI-5). Though GO was found to exhibit lower activity towards ECO2R in acetonitrile (F.E. of less than 5%), but it synergistically enhanced the ECO2R by providing support and connectivity to the Cu/CuxO present in Cu/CuxO composite.
Reduction of graphene oxide through charge transfer processes during the formation of such hybrids is well established [48–49]. The extent of defects in GO thus serves as a measure of the extent of interaction between the catalyst and GO support in such composites.
Therefore, rationalising the effect of defects in GO is mandatorily important in order to tune the catalytic (chemical as well as electrochemical) activity of the GO supported catalysts. The extent of defects in GO is usually manifested in the ratio of the intensity of D band (ID) to G band (IG), i.e. ID/IG ratio. Figure SI-5 shows an overlay of the CV curves (normalized to the peak current of pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod)) recorded over the samples with varying extent of interaction between Cu/ CuxO and GO. The sample pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) with highest ID/IG ratio was observed to exhibit lowest overpotential requirement and highest faradaic efficiency for electrochemical CO2 to CO transformation. Others to follow in the sequence of lowering activity are fCu/CuxO.GO (CFP), fCu/CuxO@GO and finally pristine GO with minimum ID/IG showing the least activity. An interesting relationship between observed peak potential (Ep) and the extent of GO defects in the Cu/ CuxO.GO composites was noticed. The Ep Vs. GO defects (presumed as a measure of Cu/CuxO -GO interactions) was observed to obey a quadratic relation; y = 0.0724x2 - 0.487x + 1.71 with R2 = 0.969 (Fig. 6). The quadratic dependence implies a strong sensitivity of electrocatalytic performance toward the GO defects. This kind of relations can prove very useful for the design of catalysts with desired durability and activity.

sections.heading: 3.2.4. Effect of oxide contents in composite
sections.text:
Another important relationship that affects the activity of electrocatalysts for ECO2R is the presence of oxide lattices in the synthesised composites. Li et al. [13] have found that presence of Cu2O layers on Cu foil electrode with a higher thickness of ≥ 3 μm results in lowering of overpotential by 0.5 V than that of polycrystalline Cu and they have attributed this mainly to the enhancement in the roughness factor of the electrode surface. On the other hand, in another study, the presence of oxides along with metal has been demonstrated to offer sites with multiple valences and hence responsible for the better catalytic activity of these nano-structures [50,51]. The presence of oxides, especially subsurface ones in a catalyst increases efficiency of metallic composites towards ECO2R. This has been ascribed to production of highly ECO2R active metastable Cu(0) or Cu(I) structures from oxide catalysts on application of negative potentials. We also found similar activity enhancement for composites with higher oxide contents than those which were predominantly metallic. In dry acetonitrile, the estimated equilibrium potential for electro-reduction of CO2 and overpotential for the formation of CO2̇̄ is reported to be +0.49 V and -1.9, respectively, by Matsubara et al. [52]. The varying extent of stabilization of the intermediate radical anion by different materials is expected to alter the magnitude of the required overpotential. It is interesting to note that the inclusion of more oxygen to copper decreases the onset potential for ECO2R, as depicted in Table 1. pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) having oxygen to Cu ratio as 1:2.8 in comparison to lower ratio of oxygen to Cu (1:4.5) in pCu/CuxO(PtRod) shows better catalytic activity in terms of decreased
overpotentials and higher faradaic efficiency for CO.

sections.heading: 3.2.5. ECO2R over pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) nano-composite
sections.text:
The above presented observations establish that among various composites synthesised for the present work, the pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) exhibits the best performance towards ECO2R. The overpotential requirement of just 550 mV for ECO2R with pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) is significantly lower than that reported with Cu based composites under similar conditions [7,14,15]. Though, still significantly higher than what is required for commercial application of CO2 sequestration, the overpotential requirement observed with Cu/CuxO.GO nano-composites in the present study is unprecedentedly the lowest to be reported so far. This enhanced activity is a collective manifestation of several aspects of GO, Cu+ sites in the subsurface oxides of Cu/CuxO and GOCu/CuxO interactions that synergistically facilitate the ECO2R. Moreover, a loose and porous morphology of pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) composite, which helps in a better diffusion of CO2 as feed for conversion can also contribute to its enhanced performance for ECO2R.
To further establish the electrochemical redox features of pCu/ CuxO.GO(PtRod), CVs were recorded in N2 saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution with potential window of +2.0 V to -0.5 V vs NHE as shown in Fig. 7 (left panel). The presented CV shows a cathodic peak and a hump, respectively at ca. 1.0 V and ca. 0.2 V vs NHE and an anodic peak located at 1.2 V vs NHE (A1). The first cathodic peak at ca. 1.0 V (C1) vs NHE could be assigned to the reduction of CuO to Cu2O whereas the second reduction peak/hump (C2) may be attributed to the reduction of Cu2O to Cuo. On scanning the potential towards positive potential an anodic peak/hump in the range of +1.1 V to +1.2 V vs NHE was noted, which can be attributed to the oxidation of the Cuo generated after reduction of Cu2O to Cuo at C2. Similar redox features have been also reported by Tang et al. [14] for copper based electrodes in 0.1 M KClO4 solution purged with N2 at pH of 10.5. The reason for lower current in peaks and humps in the present study could be the overwhelming large capacitive current due to the presence of GO sheets besides the capacitive contribution from CFP in the catalyst. These faradaic features noted in the CV recorded over pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) in N2 saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution establish the redox accessibility and redox activity of pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) catalyst.
Fig. 7 (right panel) shows an overlay of CVs recorded for pCu/ CuxO.GO(PtRod) composite sample loaded on CFP working electrode in the presence of N2 saturated (black curve) and CO2 saturated (red curve) ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 electrolyte medium. The CV corresponding to only CFP, i.e. without electro-catalyst loading (or background CV) in CO2 saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution (magenta dashed curve) is also included in the same figure. The background CV shows no Faradaic response to the presence of CO2. Similarly, the CV (black curve) corresponding to sample pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) composite in N2 saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution (i.e. no CO2 is purged in solution), shows only a slight enhancement in background current. Contrary to this, CV recorded for same electrode in CO2 saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution (red curve) shows a distinct pair of cathodic and anodic peaks
positioned at ca. -0.26 V and 0.25 V vs NHE, respectively and hence can be attributed to redox features of CO2 reduction. More importantly, the onset potential for CO formation was found to be ca. -0.07 V vs NHE which to the best of our knowledge is the lowest to be reported so far for ECO2R.
Although, the noted cathodic current for ECO2R in the form of a transient peak is not commonly noticed or reported in the literature, similar features were noted by Hori et al. [53] at metallic copper electrode in CO2 saturated phosphate solution. As per their interpretation, CO produced initially in the reduction of CO2 at - 1.01 V, is adsorbed on the electrode and interferes with the cathodic hydrogen discharge and thus lowers the cathodic current at potentials negative to - 1.01 V, resulting in a peak. This claim was supported by the fact that the Faradaic yield of H2 generated from electrolyte medium at low overpotential begins to fall after -0.90 V, where CO formation starts. The complete electrolysis current levels off at ca. -1.00 V then drops and rises again at -1.15 to -1.20 V. Thus, the adsorption of CO produced insitu from the ECO2R was attributed to the peak observed during cathodic potential scan. In our case, a peak similar to the one reported by Hori et al. [53] is observed, but the peak is comparatively much broader with less negative peak potential, i.e. at ca. -0.26 V vs NHE.
Another exciting and unprecedented feature noted during the present electrochemical studies was the appearance of a strong anodic peak positioned at ca. + 0.25 V during the reverse scan of the CVs recorded during ECO2R which can be attributed to the electro-oxidation of ECO2R products formed during the forward scan. As noted by several researchers in the past, with ACN as solvent CO happens to be the primary product along with minor products such as formates and oxalates. To verify this, CVs were recorded over the CO conditioned pCu/ CuxO.GO(PtRod) modified CFP in CO saturated ACN-0.1 M TBABF4 solution. In a typical experiment in three electrode electrochemical cell, CFP modified with pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) allowed to stand in an electrolyte solution for an hour with the continuous purging of CO, in order for it to absorb in the electrolyte medium to imitate the conditions for presence of surface adsorbed CO. For the absence of CO, the electrolyte solution was saturated with N2. As depicted in Fig. 8, no anodic peak of whatsoever nature was observed in the CVs recorded in the absence of CO (black curve) but for CO-saturated electrolyte solution, presence of an anodic peak located at +0.18 V vs NHE which is closer to the position of anodic peak observed during ECO2R is noted in CV (red curve). The slight difference in the peak positions can be attributed to the differing strength of CO adsorption under these two different circumstances. The CO oxidation peak lowers in the second scan of CV (red curve) indicating lowering of adsorbed CO at the electrode surface. The peak potential corresponding to electro-oxidation of CO adsorbed after purging (+0.18 V vs NHE) is ca. 80 mV lower than the one corresponding to CO adsorbed during ECO2R (+0.26 V vs NHE).
In light of these observations, the anodic peak observed in the present study can be attributed to the oxidation of CO generated at the electrode surface during ECO2R. Such kind of features, i.e. oxidation of adsorbed CO generated during methanol oxidation on Pt surfaces is a
commonly noted phenomenon in electrochemical studies on methanol oxidation reactions. Similar observations of strong adsorption of CO generated during CO2 reduction on Pt and Cu metal surfaces are also reported by Hori et al. [53]. They observed an anodic current at ca. + 0.3 V vs RHE, probably owing to anodic oxidation of adsorbed CO on the Pt electrode. Incidentally, the anodic peak position, i.e., +0.25 V vs NHE observed in present study is very close to the value reported by Hori et al. [53]; the minor difference could be due to the difference in catalyst surface used in these two different studies. Similar behaviour has been reported by Torelli et al. on NixGay catalysts [54] where an intense anodic peak at +0.54 V vs RHE on the return scan after CO2 reduction electrolysis in 0.1 M KHCO3 and attributed it to oxidation of CO or another chemisorbed CO2 reduction intermediate.

sections.heading: 3.3. Analysis of the reaction products
sections.text:
The above mentioned claims that we propose for the interpretation of the observations vis a vis the voltammetric investigations are further supported by the ECO2R product analysis investigations. Since, the main aim was to improve the efficiency of the crafted composites for the electro-production of CO, an essential component of synthetic gas (CO + H2), a precursor for the industrial Fisher-Tropsh process; we limited the analysis to the gaseous phase products only. Typically, in a 3-electrode airtight single chamber electrochemical cell equipped with electro-catalyst modified CFP as working electrode, the cell contents were saturated with CO2 gas. After initial purging for 30 minutes, the potential of the working electrode was stepped to a potential ca. 20 mV more negative to the ECO2R peak position observed for the CO2 reduction over the said electrode and a chronoamperogram was recorded while the cell contents were continuously purged with CO2 at a controlled flow rate of 5 cubic centimetre per minute. The gaseous products from ECO2R were collected in a Tedlar bag (different bags for different electrode surfaces) attached to the electrochemical cell through one of its necks. For instance, pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) sample modified electrode, a chrono-amperometric scan at an applied potential of -0.28 V vs NHE (20 mV higher than peak potential) was run for an hour. Similar assembly, procedures, and cell were used for the rest of the electro-catalyst materials.
The composition of gaseous products as established by GC was found to be predominantly CO along with traces of C2H6 that corresponds to faradaic efficiencies of 40% and 4%, respectively. Fig. 9 depicts faradaic efficiencies of the gaseous products formed during electrolysis of CO2 saturated electrolyte solution using different electrocatalyst modified electrodes. All the studied samples show production of CO as a major product and in accordance to their CV response. pCu/
CuxO(PtRod) modified electrodes showed second best faradaic efficiency of 25% towards CO production along with 8% F.E. for methane. For rest of the samples (i.e., with CFP as a cathode), the faradaic efficiencies for CO were observed to be in the range of only 14-16% which is much lower than the one obtained with the electro-catalysts prepared using Pt rod as cathode during electrochemical deposition.
Use of platinum as a quasi-reference (QRE) for bulk electrolysis has been a point of debate, though thoroughly researched by Kasem et al. [55] that Pt can be used without much error as a QRE for these type of studies. To ascertain the same, we checked the stability of the Pt as QRE at regular intervals during 3900 secs long voltammetric experiment. For this, we recorded the redox behaviour of the ferrocene/ferrocenium couple over a Pt plate with Pt mesh as counter and Pt employed in the electrolysis experiments as QRE or an Ag/AgCl (double junction) as reference electrode in a cell with 5 mM ferrocene dissolved in the acetonitrile containing 100 mM TBABF4 that was degassed by argon purging for 10 minutes. A CV was recorded in beginning of the experiment, and the same was repeated post-2000, 3500 and 3900 seconds of Pt QRE`s use in the bulk analysis [55]. Figure SI-6 depicts the redox peaks of the ferrocene analyte species during long electrolysis experiments run for 3900 seconds. It clearly shows that the potential of Pt QRE shows a negligible shift in the characteristic peak positions. Similar minor shift was also observed with commercial Ag/AgCl reference electrode during electrolysis experiment. This shows that Pt can be used as QRE in our system and other organic systems within experimental timeline without introduction of any significant error [55].
Both theoretical [56] and experimental [53,57,58] investigations have established that the reduction of CO2 to CO comprises the first and the rate-determining step for ECO2R to hydrocarbons over Cu. As reported earlier, ECO2R in ACN medium follows Amatore − Savéant mechanism [59], according to which ECO2R in solvents of low proton availability such as dimethylformamide and ACN involves three competing pathways: oxalate formation through self-coupling of the CO2-. anion radicals, CO formation via oxygen-carbon coupling of CO2-. with CO2, and formate formation through protonation of CO2-. by residual water followed by homogeneous electron transfer from CO2-.. The critical steps of the reduction process involve initial electron transfer which is also the rate determining step for these three competing pathways for ECO2R. Recently, Figueiredo et al. [43] with the help of spectro-electrochemical measurements on ECO2R on Cu electrodes in ACN solution have demonstrated that for the presence of trace amounts of water, the main reaction products from ECO2R are carbonates, bicarbonate, and CO. Thus, the production of methane and ethane along with CO in the present study can be attributed to the presence of
residual water in ACN solution which was stated to be ca. 1000 ppm by the supplier of the HPLC grade ACN used for the present investigations. Moreover, it is pertinent to mention here that ACN has a high tendency to absorb moisture when exposed to laboratory environment during transfer and handling.
On prima-facie, the analysis of the trend in variation of faradaic efficiencies of the ECO2R products looks complex and seems that probably a combination of several factors dictates the mechanistic aspects of ECO2R. Overall, we observed that four factors viz. (i) procedure employed for electrode fabrication, (ii) choice of the cathode in electrochemical synthesis, Pt vs CFP, (iii) GO support and the extent of its reduction, and (iv) an extent of oxide contents in Cu2O.GO nano-composite play a significant role in deciding the fate of the reaction products. Amongst the studied samples, Cu/CuxO.GO composite obtained using Pt cathode during electrochemical deposition in the presence of GO contains highest oxide contents and maximum interaction between metal oxide and GO support, was observed to exhibit the highest faradaic efficiency of 40% for conversion of CO2 to CO, explicitly demonstrating the role of GO, oxide phase, collection substrate and strategy. A comparative account of the onset potentials and the F.E. values observed for the Cu/CuxO.GO nanocomposite crafted for the present work and those reported for the various state of the art electrocatalysts toward ECO2R in CO2-saturated aprotic/organic/ionic liquid solutions are presented as Table 2. The entries in Table 2 establish that the electrocatalytic performance of pCu/CuxO.GO(PtRod) nanocomposite toward ECO2R is superior to many state of the art electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
Precisely, for the present study, we succeeded in crafting a Cu/ CuxO.GO composite through a simple, efficient, and economical electrodeposition that exhibit a higher F. E. with very low over potentials for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. Our results show that we could achieve unprecedented lowest to be onset potential for reduction of CO2 with an impressive 40% F. E. towards CO. The presented results establish that the manifestation of several parameters including oxide contents in an electrocatalyst, interaction of the support (GO) with the Cu-nanostructures and the mode of fabrication employed to construct the working electrodes along with morphology and porous nature of the nano-composite contribute crucially towards efficient CO2 electro-reduction. We demonstrated that an industry friendly catalyst could be crafted by precisely choosing efficiently interacting support, presence of metal cations to stabilise the negative radical intermediate in ECO2R and an asymmetric nano-morphology. These results, we believe, are going to open new ways to design, craft simple, economic and robust catalysts for ECO2R.
